raw_case_text:
The patient was a 65-year-old male farmer that worked primarily on corn and bean crops but also raised a few dairy cows. He was born and lived in Camara, a rural area of the Uruburetama mountains, and denied traveling outside Ceara State or living in other locations, nor did he come in contact with armadillos.
The patient sought for care on September 8, 2016 at the outpatient clinic of Systemic Mycoses of the Sao Jose Hospital of Infectious Diseases, in Fortaleza, Ceara State, complaining of an oral inflammation that had been upsetting him during the past three years. Fever or respiratory symptoms were not reported. The infiltrative oral lesion was located on the palate (Figure 1). In addition, an ulcerative lesion was found on the skin and right nasal mucosa (Figure 2). Hypophonetic cardiac sounds and reduced vesicular murmurs in both lungs were also found. The abdominal examination was normal, and cervical lymph node enlargement was not observed. The patient reported cigarette consumption of 40 packs/year for 40 years but had stopped smoking that past year. After undergoing a chest X-ray, nodules with predominantly central distribution were observed affecting both lungs, some showing signs of cavitation and bilateral perihilar reticular infiltrate (Figure 3).
A previous biopsy of the hard palate lesion revealed a squamous pattern of mucosal fragments presenting granulation tissue associated with chronic lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and multinucleated cells, with cytoplasmic inclusions compatible with a fungal infection, evidenced by PAS and Grocott stains, suggestive of Paracoccidioides spp. yeast forms. Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the face revealed a maxillo-ethmoidal sinusopathy, left-deviated bone septum, palatine bulging to the right and an irregularity of the cortical bone of the hard palate on the left side. An imprint of the palatal lesion showed a moderate presence of intra- and extracellular yeast structures with considerably variable sizes (small and oval, medium, large and rounded) by Giemsa staining; Leishmania was not found in the analyzed material.
A new biopsy was performed for microbiological examination and treatment with itraconazole (200 mg daily) was initiated at the same day the patient was first seen at Sao Jose Hospital. P. brasiliensis was identified by the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) after fungi growth in culture. For species identification, DNA extraction of yeast cells was performed, based on a previous protocol with minor modifications, using the DNeasy Plant Mini Kit (Qiagen , USA). The obtained product was subjected to PCR using panfungal primers ITS1 (5'-TCCGTAGGTGAACCTG CGG-3') and ITS4 (5'-TCCTCCGCTTATTGATATGC-3'). The final 25 muL of PCR mix was composed of 2.95 muL of ultrapure water, 5.0 muL of buffer (Promega, Madison, Wisconsin, USA), 5.0 muL of MgCl2 (Promega, Madison, Wisconsin, USA), 5.0 muL of dNTP (Promega, Madison, Wisconsin, USA), 2.5 muL of each primer (Invitrogen, Thermo Scientific, Waltham, Massachusetts, USA), 0.05 muL of Go Hot Start Taq polymerase (Promega, Madison, Wisconsin, USA), and 2.0 muL of DNA template. PCR conditions were: initial denaturation at 95  C for 5 min, followed by 30 cycles of 95  C for 20 s, annealing at 56  C for 15 s, and extension at 72  C for 65 s, and a final extension step at 72  C for 5 min. The presence of PCR products (639 bp) was verified in 1% agarose gel electrophoresis. Then, amplicons were sequenced and compared with the P. brasiliensis CBS 372.73 strain (GenBank accession MH860706.1) using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (Nucleotide Blast ), resulting in the identification of P. brasiliensis with 98.8% of similarity.
Double radial immunodiffusion for PCM was positive. The patient was treated with itraconazole for 17 months and evolved with lesion improvement. A white scar over his hard palate caused a retraction in the tonsil topography, but there was no clinical disturbance. The individual had a normal chest X-ray at the end of treatment and had also undergone a new CT scan of the face, which showed a sinusopathy and left-deviated bone septum, but did not evidence the previous bone alterations in the palatal region. He was followed-up until June 6, 2019, persisting free of symptoms.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male farmer from rural Ceara State, Brazil, presented in September 2016 with a 3-year history of a painful infiltrative palatal lesion and ulcerative nasal mucosal and cutaneous lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 3 years prior to presentation at Sao Jose Hospital of Infectious Diseases in Fortaleza, the patient experienced persistent oral inflammation on his hard palate accompanied by ulcerative lesions of the nasal mucosa and adjacent skin, without fever or respiratory complaints.
subjective.past_medical_history: Lifelong resident and corn/bean/dairy farmer in Camara (Uruburetama mountains, Ceara State, Brazil) with no travel outside Ceara and no armadillo contact; former heavy smoker (40 pack-years, quit 1 year prior).
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for fever or respiratory symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Infiltrative granulomatous mucosal lesion on the hard palate and an ulcerative lesion involving the right nasal mucosa and adjacent skin; hypophonetic heart sounds and bilaterally decreased vesicular breath sounds; normal abdominal exam and no cervical lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral central-predominant pulmonary nodules (some cavitary) and bilateral perihilar reticular infiltrates. Double radial immunodiffusion serology was positive for paracoccidioidomycosis.
objective.advanced_workup: Facial CT showed maxillo-ethmoidal sinusopathy, leftward bony nasal septal deviation, rightward palatal bulging, and left hard-palate cortical bone irregularity. Giemsa-stained palatal lesion imprint showed variably sized intra- and extracellular yeast cells without Leishmania amastigotes; hard palate biopsy (H&E, PAS, and Grocott stains) revealed chronic granulomatous lymphohistiocytic and multinucleated giant-cell inflammation containing fungal yeast inclusions. Culture and panfungal ITS1/ITS4 PCR (639-bp amplicon) with sequencing confirmed Paracoccidioides brasiliensis (98.8% identity to strain CBS 372.73).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis was excluded by negative Giemsa imprint and histopathology; PAS/Grocott staining, double radial immunodiffusion, fungal culture, and ITS1/ITS4 PCR sequencing confirmed chronic multifocal (pulmonary and mucocutaneous) paracoccidioidomycosis caused by Paracoccidioides brasiliensis. A 17-month course of oral itraconazole (200 mg/day) achieved complete healing of the palatal and nasal lesions (leaving only a benign palatal scar), normalization of the chest radiograph, resolution of palatal bone erosion on repeat facial CT, and symptom-free survival through June 2019.
